ideas.name: Scrambling data in transit
ideas.question: Why does HTTPS make your traffic safe on café Wi-Fi?
ideas.modelAnswer: Both ends encrypt the data, so anyone in the middle only sees scrambled bytes. They can tell you are exchanging data, but not what it says.

whenOptions.text: Hiding which website you visited from your network
Checking whether a shop is honest
Typing a password while on café Wi-Fi

ideas.misread: I scramble the data so nobody knows I'm online at all! Poof, invisible me!

ideas.name: Secret key handshake
ideas.question: How can a browser and server share a secret key without sending it openly?
ideas.modelAnswer: In the handshake, each side contributes a random value and both compute the same session key using a key exchange. An eavesdropper who sees everything still cannot work it out.
keyPoints: Same key computed on both sides

whenOptions.text: Noticing someone changed a page's contents
Two strangers agreeing on a secret in a crowded room
Proving a website belongs to your bank

ideas.misread: The browser writes the key on a note and sends it very quietly. Shhh!

ideas.name: Certificates prove identity
ideas.question: Why does your browser check a certificate during the handshake?
ideas.modelAnswer: A certificate, signed by a trusted authority, says the key belongs to the real site. This stops someone on the network from pretending to be your bank.

whenOptions.text: Making sure you're really on your bank's site
Detecting a changed bit in a download
Scrambling the data after the connection starts

ideas.misread: A certificate is a gold star! Any site with one is honest and nice, I'm sure.

ideas.name: Tamper detection
ideas.question: How does HTTPS notice if someone alters data on the way?
ideas.modelAnswer: Each piece of encrypted data carries a tamper seal. If even one bit changes, the check fails and the connection is dropped.

whenOptions.text: Choosing a strong password for your account
Stopping a network from injecting ads into pages
Hiding the site name from your provider

ideas.misread: If someone changes a bit, I just glue it back and carry on! Good as new!

ideas.name: What padlock doesn't promise
ideas.question: Why doesn't the padlock mean a website is trustworthy?
ideas.modelAnswer: HTTPS protects the content of the connection, not the fact you visited or the site's honesty. A scam site can have a valid certificate, so it only means the connection is private to the domain's owner.

whenOptions.text: Verifying a signature chain to an authority
Reading messages sent over open Wi-Fi
Deciding not to trust a shop just because of its padlock

ideas.misread: Padlock means the website is a good guy and totally hides that I visited it!

i1.say: Ooh, so both the computer and the website wrap their messages up tight before they leave, like sealing letters in a box! Anyone peeking along the way just sees a squiggly mess of bytes, like gibberish soup.
i1.example: Oh! So my computer and the website both lock the data before it travels, and anyone listening only hears a jumble of nonsense bytes. It's like a locked box in the post, and I'd squish the postman's ears flat trying to read it!
i1.whenRight: Oh! So when I type my password at the café, the scrambling keeps it safe from the Wi-Fi snoopers? I see now: only jumbled bytes reach them, never my secret words. Thank you, coach!
i1.whenWrong: Hmm, I don't think that's quite it! Your coach said the scrambling hides what the data says, not whether I visited the site. Could the scramble hide the visit too? I'm just a blot, so I'm not sure.
i1.checkRight: So both my computer and the website lock the data before it zooms along the wires, meaning a snooper just sees scrambled gibberish, like a letter in a locked box that the postman can't read. Right?
i1.why: Ooh, so both of us lock our words into a wiggly jumble before they zoom off, and a snoop on the line just sees squiggles that mean nothing, like alphabet soup nobody can spoon! Because people sharing the Wi-Fi can copy traffic, the lock keeps passwords safe even when they're peeking.
i1.whyAsk: But WHY does scrambling the data keep it safe on café Wi-Fi, coach? Like, if the Wi-Fi people can see the jumble, what stops them from unscrambling it too?
i1.fixed: Oh! So the jumble is only for reading, not for hiding that I'm visiting. Watchers still see my knock at the door, they just can't read the note I pass through the mail slot. Phew, I finally get it!

i2.say: Ooh, so at the very start, each of us picks a random number like tossing a dice in secret, and then some clever math lets us both end up holding the exact same secret key. I'd wobble like jelly trying to juggle that many numbers!
i2.example: Oooh, so each side picks a secret random number of its own, and by a clever mixing trick they both end up with the exact same secret key! Like two friends mixing paint, I'm told, so they match perfectly, Coach!
i2.whenRight: Oooh, so two strangers in a crowded room each pick a secret number and, by a clever trick, end up with the very same secret key, even though the crowd is listening! I would use that whenever two sides have never met but need a private code of their own.
i2.whenWrong: Hmm, I don't think that's the right fit, Coach. Changing a page's contents is a different trick, not the handshake. Could you tell me more about how the two sides first agree on their secret?
i2.checkRight: Ooh, so at the start, each side picks a random value of its own. Then, like mixing paint, they swap their colors and both end up with the exact same secret shade, the session key. Right?
i2.why: Oooh, so each side tosses in a random value, and with a special key-making trick they both end up holding the very same secret! And since the key never travels openly, a spy watching everything still can't rebuild it, and a brand new key each visit keeps things safe. I feel like a tiny ink-blot secret keeper!
i2.whyAsk: But WHY can't the eavesdropper work out the secret, even after watching the whole handshake? How does the math keep it hidden from them?
i2.fixed: Oh! So the key was never a note passed under the table, I was picturing it all wrong. Both of us just do a little math dance with random bits and somehow end up holding the very same secret, while anyone watching only sees the steps. Phew, my ink is less soggy now!

i3.say: Ooh, so a certificate is a signed note from a trusted grown-up saying this key belongs to this website name, so I know who I'm really talking to! It's like a name tag I can check, Coach, even if the monster wears a fake mustache.
i3.example: Ooh, so a certificate is a signed paper saying "this key belongs to this website name," and a trusted authority stamps it! My ink-brain pictures a passport: the name has to match the face, so no sneaky impostor gets through the border.
i3.whenRight: Oh! So a certificate is like a signed ID card, and when I visit my bank, my browser checks that card so I'm not chatting with a sneaky impostor. Is that why the bank's site gets a padlock and a dodgy one gets a scary warning?
i3.whenWrong: Hmm, I don't think that's the one, my coach! A bit changing in a download sounds more like a tamper seal to me, not a certificate. Try another situation for me?
i3.checkRight: So a certificate is a paper that says this key belongs to this website's name, and a trusted authority signed it, like a stamp. And like a passport, the name has to match the one I'm talking to, so no stranger can pretend to be my bank. Right?
i3.why: Oh! So a certificate is a signed paper saying this key belongs to this website's name, vouched for by someone trusted. Then I know who I'm really chatting with, so the impostor can't sneak in like a crumb in my pocket!
i3.whyAsk: But WHY does my browser even bother checking that paper during the handshake, coach? Is it trying to catch a sneaky pretender before we say anything secret?
i3.fixed: Oh! So a certificate is just a signed note saying this key belongs to this name, not a gold star for being nice. Phew, I thought the site was a good little citizen. I'll remember: it proves who owns the name, nothing more!

i4.say: Oooh, so every little bundle of scrambled stuff wears a tiny seal, like a wax stamp on a letter! If even one single bit gets poked, the seal breaks and the whole connection gets snipped shut.
i4.example: Ooh, so every bit of scrambled data wears a tiny tamper seal! If even one bit gets changed, the seal breaks and the connection gets snipped shut, like a jar lid that pops its button. I would throw that jar away too!
i4.whenRight: Oh! So if a sneaky network tries to slip ads into my page, the tamper seal catches the change and cuts the connection, like a jar lid that pops if someone fiddles with it! I would use that whenever a network might meddle with a page on its way to me.
i4.whenWrong: Hmm, I don't think that's it, coach! A strong password is about guarding your account, not about spotting a changed bit. My brain is still wobbling on this, so tell me more about the seal?
i4.checkRight: So every bit of scrambled data wears a tamper seal, like a jar lid with a popped safety button! If even one bit gets changed, the seal breaks and the connection gets cut off. Right?
i4.why: Oh! So every bit of encrypted data wears a little tamper seal, like a wax stamp on a letter. If even one dot gets smudged, the whole connection gets snipped shut, and nobody can secretly swap your payment amount!
i4.whyAsk: But WHY does the tamper seal break if just one tiny bit changes, coach? Does it count every bit like a tiny sheep?
i4.fixed: Oh! So a broken seal means the whole connection gets dropped, I can't just patch the bit back! I finally get it now, phew. Thank you, coach, that one nearly soaked me!

i5.say: So the padlock means my chat with the site is private, just between me and whoever owns that domain! But it doesn't tell me if that owner is nice, like a locked box might still hold a sneaky goblin inside.
i5.example: Oh! So the padlock only means my visit is private, like a sealed letter, but it doesn't mean the person who wrote the letter is nice. A scam shoe shop can wear a padlock too, and my network can still see I knocked on its door!
i5.whenRight: Oh! So the padlock is like a locked box delivered only to the shop, but a sneaky shop can still lock up a bad box! I should not trust a shop just because of its padlock, right?
i5.whenWrong: Hmm, my coach, I think that card is a different puzzle piece! The padlock talk is about privacy and not about trust, so the signature chain card doesn't quite fit here. Could we try another one?
i5.checkRight: The padlock only means my chat with that site is private, between me and whoever owns the domain. It doesn't mean the owner is good, like a scam shoe shop still getting a padlock. Right?
i5.why: Ooh, so the padlock only keeps my chat private between me and whoever owns the website, like a sealed letter that still tells the postman who it's for. It doesn't tell me if that owner is a nice one, so I have to decide that myself!
i5.whyAsk: But WHY doesn't the padlock mean the site is honest, coach? Couldn't a sneaky site just wear the padlock like a fancy hat?
i5.fixed: Oh! So the padlock only keeps my words private, like a sealed letter, but it never promises the mailman is nice or hides that I sent a letter at all. Got it, phew!

i1.say: Both my computer and the website lock the data before it travels, so anyone listening along the way just sees a jumble of meaningless bytes.
i1.example: It's like mailing a letter in a locked box: the postman sees the box and who it's going to, but can't read the letter.
i1.why: People on shared networks can copy traffic, so scrambling keeps passwords and messages private even if someone is snooping.
i1.fix: No, it does not make me invisible online. Watchers can still tell I'm talking to someone, but they can't read what the data says.

i2.say: At the start, each side picks a random value, and using a key exchange trick both work out the very same secret session key.
i2.example: Like two friends mixing paint colors: each adds a private color to a shared one, swaps the mix, and both end with the same final shade.
i2.why: The key never travels openly, so a spy watching everything still can't rebuild it, and a fresh key each visit limits damage.
i2.fix: No, the browser does not write the key on a note and send it quietly. Both sides compute the same key from exchanged values, so it is never sent.

i3.say: A certificate is a document signed by a trusted authority saying this key really belongs to this website name, so I know who I'm talking to.
i3.example: It's like a passport checked by border officers: the name must match the person, so a stranger can't claim to be my bank.
i3.why: Without proof of identity, someone on the network could pose as the site, and my encrypted chat would go straight to the impostor.
i3.fix: No, a certificate is not a gold star for being honest or nice. It only proves the site owns that name, not that its owners behave well.

i4.say: Every chunk of encrypted data comes with a tamper seal, and if even one bit is altered, the check fails and the connection gets cut off.
i4.example: It's like a jar lid with a safety button: if the button is popped, you know someone opened it and you throw the jar away.
i4.why: This stops attackers from quietly changing messages in transit, like swapping a payment amount, because any change is noticed immediately.
i4.fix: No, I can't glue a changed bit back and carry on. A failed check means the data is untrustworthy, so the connection is dropped.

i5.say: The padlock means the content of my connection is private between me and the domain's owner, but it says nothing about whether that owner is good.
i5.example: A scam site pretending to sell cheap shoes can still show a padlock, and my visit to it is still known by my network.
i5.why: Encryption and certificates only guard the contents and the identity of the domain, so I still have to judge honesty and trust myself.
i5.fix: No, the padlock does not mean the website is a good guy or hides that I visited. It only keeps the content private; the visit is still visible.
